input.title: Powerhouse runs two authorization systems that both call their unit a grant: the host's permission tables at the GraphQL boundary, and the document's own auth scope inside the reactor

input.description: A permission is a READ/WRITE/ADMIN row in a host database, enforced when serving GraphQL and sync; a grant is an operation folded into the document. A write passes the tables first, then the policy.

Extracted from apps/academy/docs/academy/03-Build/03-BuildingUserExperiences/07-Authorization/02-DocumentPermissions.md at v6.2.2-dev.74 — same info box; 'Both call their unit a grant, and they are not the same thing'

input.content:
Two mechanisms decide authorization, they answer different questions, and neither replaces the other. The v6.2.2-dev.74 Academy adds the same callout to both permission pages to keep them apart:

| | Host-side permission tables | Document auth scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | Database tables owned by the reactor host (Switchboard) | The document's `auth` scope, replicated with it |
| Unit | A READ / WRITE / ADMIN level (plus operation rows) | A grant: principal × capability × effect |
| Enforced | At the GraphQL boundary and when serving sync | Inside the reactor at admission, replay and read |
| Status | What a deployment runs today | Staged behind feature flags |
| Question | Which addresses does this host let near a drive or document? | Who may do what to this document, everywhere it replicates? |

A GraphQL write passes the tables **first**, and then the document's own policy where enforcement is enabled. The tables cannot be replicated (they are private to one host), which is exactly why the reactor-level rule exists: a decision made from host-local data cannot be verified by a replica, so it can gate a request but never change how an operation is evaluated inside the reactor.

The spec's stages 8–10 are the planned convergence: sync serving moves onto the policy (8), the tables are expressed as grants (9), and the host stops consulting them on the read path (10). Until then `authEnforcement` cannot be turned on for a fleet that relies on the tables, because every existing document's policy is uninitialized and therefore open. One thing does not port: node-local administrators, which the reactor has no concept of — an administrator who could read past a document's policy at the host while the reactor denies the same read is an inconsistency, not a feature.
